content: Premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) is a condition characterized by severe symptoms of depression, irritability, and tension that occur before menstruation. These symptoms are significantly more intense than those associated with premenstrual syndrome (PMS). PMS encompasses a variety of physical and emotional symptoms that typically manifest 5 to 11 days before the onset of menstruation and usually resolve once menstruation begins or shortly thereafter. Symptoms of PMDD: The symptoms of PMDD resemble those of PMS but are more severe and debilitating. They include at least one mood-related symptom and occur during the week leading up to menstruation, improving within a few days after the period starts. To diagnose PMDD, at least five of the following symptoms must be present, including one mood-related symptom: Loss of interest in daily activities and relationships. Fatigue or low energy levels. Feelings of sadness or hopelessness, potentially accompanied by suicidal thoughts. Persistent tension or anxiety. A sense of being out of control. Food cravings or episodes of binge eating. Mood swings, often marked by periods of tearfulness. Panic attacks. Persistent irritability or anger that impacts others. Physical symptoms such as bloating, breast tenderness, headaches, and joint or muscle pain. Sleep disturbances. Difficulty concentrating. Causes of PMDD: The exact causes of PMDD and PMS remain unknown. However, hormonal changes during the menstrual cycle are believed to play a significant role. PMDD affects approximately 3% to 8% of women during their reproductive years. Many women with PMDD also experience conditions such as: Anxiety. Major depression. Seasonal affective disorder (SAD). Other contributing factors may include: Alcohol abuse. Being overweight. High caffeine consumption. A family history of the disorder, particularly in the mother. Lack of regular exercise. When to Seek Urgent Medical Care: If you are experiencing suicidal thoughts, call 911 or a local crisis line immediately. Schedule an appointment with your healthcare provider if: Symptoms do not improve with self-treatment. Symptoms interfere with your daily life. Diagnosis: There are no specific physical examinations or laboratory tests to diagnose PMDD. A thorough medical history, physical examination (including a pelvic exam), and psychiatric evaluation are necessary to rule out other conditions. Keeping a calendar or diary of symptoms can help women identify the most troublesome symptoms and their timing, which can assist healthcare providers in diagnosing PMDD and determining the most effective treatment. Treatment Options: Managing PMDD begins with adopting a healthy lifestyle. Recommendations include: Eating a balanced diet rich in whole grains, vegetables, and fruits, while minimizing salt, sugar, alcohol, and caffeine intake. Engaging in regular aerobic exercise throughout the month to reduce the severity of PMS symptoms. Adjusting sleep habits before considering medications for insomnia. Keeping a diary or calendar to record: The type of symptoms experienced. Their severity. Their duration. Antidepressants may be beneficial, with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) being the first-line option. SSRIs can be taken during the second half of the menstrual cycle until menstruation begins or throughout the entire month. Consult your doctor for guidance. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) may also be used, either alone or in combination with antidepressants. CBT typically involves about 10 sessions with a mental health professional over several weeks. Other potential treatments include: Birth control pills (oral contraceptives), which may either alleviate or exacerbate PMS symptoms, including depression. Diuretics for women who experience significant weight gain due to fluid retention. Nutritional supplements such as vitamin B6, calcium, and magnesium. Medications like Depo-Lupron, which suppress ovarian function and ovulation. Pain relievers such as aspirin or ibuprofen for headaches, backaches, menstrual cramps, and breast tenderness. Prognosis: With proper diagnosis and treatment, most women with PMDD find that their symptoms either resolve or become manageable to a tolerable degree. Possible Complications: PMDD symptoms can be severe enough to disrupt a woman’s daily life. Women with depression may experience worsening symptoms during the second half of their menstrual cycle, potentially requiring adjustments to their medication. Up to 10% of women reporting PMS symptoms, particularly those with PMDD, have experienced suicidal thoughts. Suicide in women with depression is more likely to occur during the second half of the menstrual cycle. PMDD may also be associated with eating disorders and smoking.
